purpose: Thioridazine is used to treat schizophrenia, specifically in patients who have not responded to other antipsychotic medicines. It helps reduce symptoms like hallucinations, confused thinking, and unusual behaviors. Because of its serious risks, it is generally only used as a last resort.
how_it_works: Thioridazine works by blocking certain chemical messengers in the brain, mainly dopamine, which can become overactive in conditions like schizophrenia. By calming down this overactivity, it helps reduce disturbing thoughts, hallucinations, and agitation. Think of it like turning down the volume on brain signals that are too loud.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, weight gain, low blood pressure when standing up (which can cause lightheadedness), and difficulty urinating. Some people may also notice stiffness or muscle movements they cannot control.
warnings: IMPORTANT: Thioridazine can cause a serious and potentially life-threatening heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation. It can also cause permanent eye damage (pigmentary retinopathy) affecting your vision, especially at higher doses. It must NOT be used with many other medications. Elderly patients with dementia have a higher risk of death with this type of drug. Regular eye exams and heart monitoring (EKG) are required. Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines you take.
typical_dosing: Doses are usually started low, around 50 mg taken 2 to 3 times a day, and may be adjusted by your doctor based on your response. The total daily dose typically ranges from 200 mg to 800 mg per day, divided into several doses. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes — never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
